title: Queue-shape-aware sizing probe (continuous batching + concurrency)
content:
Context and goal:

This is a lightweight spreadsheet-first probe into how queue shape (burstiness, tail of inter-arrival times) interacts with continuous batching and slot-concurrency policies to produce p95 latency and unit GPU cost. The immediate goal is: given workload arrival shape + per-token model cost curve, produce a small set of sizing knobs (min_slots, max_slots, batch_window_ms, slot_size_tokens) and a recommended default policy that hits target p95 <= 250 ms for 90% of traffic profiles while minimizing GPU-seconds/token.

Why this is different from prior notes:
- Instead of assuming Poisson or steady stream, we explicitly parameterize queue shape with a 3-parameter mixture: steady-rate, short bursts (microbursts), and long-tail occasional spikes.
- We model continuous batching as a leaky-bucket producer: the batch emission time is either batch_window_ms or when slot is full (token budget), whichever comes first, and we propagate queueing delay into p95 with percentiles computed from empirical arrival shape.
- We include a sanity spreadsheet layout and example numeric outputs so SRE/infra can reproduce quickly.

High-level modeling approach (spreadsheet tabs)
- Tab: params (single-cell knobs)
  - target_p95_ms: 250
  - slot_size_tokens: 2048 (tokens per slot)
  - batch_window_ms: 12
  - per_token_latency_ms: function of model and sequence length (see latency_curve tab)
  - concurrency_slots: variable to sweep (min..max)
  - gpu_cost_per_hour: $3.60 (placeholder)

- Tab: arrival_shapes (sampled quantiles)
  - steady_rate_rps: baseline throughput in requests/s
  - burst_fraction: fraction of traffic in short bursts (0..1)
  - burst_peak_multiplier: multiplier relative to steady (e.g., 5x)
  - tail_spike_rate: events/day and spike_multiplier (e.g., 1/day, 20x)
  - empirical inter-arrival percentiles: columns at p50/p90/p99/p999 (for synthetic generator)

- Tab: latency_curve
  - simple per-token model latency = base_ms + per_token_ms * tokens_generated (use bench curves from /benchmarks)
  - example: base 12 ms, per_token 1.5 ms for CPU baseline, per_token 0.38 ms for quantized A100 run (numbers illustrative)

- Tab: sim_runs
  - each row = one scenario (combination of arrival shape + slot sizing + batch window)
  - columns: scenario_id, steady_rps, burst_fraction, burst_multiplier, min_slots, max_slots, batch_window_ms, slot_tokens, mean_latency_ms, p50_queue_ms, p95_queue_ms, effective_p95_end_to_end_ms, gpu_seconds_per_1M_tokens, unit_cost_per_1k_tokens

Queue-shape modeling details
- Queueing delay per request is modeled as additive: queue_delay = time until next batch emission + time waiting for concurrency slot to execute.
- Batch emission distribution: for arrival pattern A(t), the residual time to batch depends on arrival since last emission. For small batch_window_ms (< 20 ms) we approximate residual distribution with uniform(0,batch_window_ms) for steady arrivals and shift toward 0 when burst occupancy is high.
- Concurrency slot wait: if all slots busy, requests accumulate in a queue ordered by emission time. We approximate slot occupancy with an M/G/k-like occupancy curve but inject a conservative fudge factor: occupancy_effective = theoretical_util * (1 + burst_amplification_factor).
- For numeric simplicity in the sheet, we compute p95_queue_ms by sampling 10k synthetic arrivals (fast vectorized) using the mixture distribution (steady + microbursts + rare spikes) and applying deterministic batch emission rules. This avoids closed-form complexity and matches experiment.

Key equations used (spreadsheet formulas)
- batch_fill_time_est = min(batch_window_ms, slot_tokens / expected_tokens_per_emit_at_time_t)
- mean_service_ms = latency_curve(tokens_per_req)
- service_time_per_slot_ms = mean_service_ms * concurrent_requests_per_slot_factor
- utilization = offered_work_ms / (n_slots * slot_cycle_ms)
- p95_end_to_end = p95_queue_ms + p95_service_ms (service tail approximated with +1.3 * mean_service for p95 in small samples)

Example scenarios (rows copied from sheet):
1) Baseline steady stream
- steady_rps = 40 req/s, average tokens_out = 64, burst_fraction=0, slot_tokens=2048, batch_window=12 ms, min_slots=2, max_slots=4
- sim outputs: p95_queue_ms = 14 ms, mean_service_ms = 55 ms, effective_p95_end_to_end_ms = 84 ms, gpu_seconds_per_1M_tokens = 0.98, cost_per_1k_tokens = $0.0035

2) Microburst-heavy (user typing bursts)
- steady_rps = 12, burst_fraction=0.35, burst_multiplier=6x, tail_spike_rate=0/day
- sim outputs with same slots: p95_queue_ms = 210 ms (due to slot queuing), mean_service_ms = 52 ms, effective_p95_end_to_end_ms = 262 ms (misses 250 ms target)
- sensitivity shows doubling min_slots to 4 reduces p95_queue to 62 ms, end-to-end p95=114 ms but increases GPU-seconds/token by ~28%

3) Rare large spike (external event)
- spike 1/day, multiplier 30x, short duration 3s
- with auto-scale headroom (max_slots=12) p95 remains <= 320 ms for 99.5% of traffic; without burst headroom p95 explodes > 2s for affected requests.

Policy recommendations (practical knobs)
- Default conservative profile for customer tiers with p95 target 250 ms:
  - slot_tokens: 2048, batch_window: 12 ms, min_slots: ceil(steady_rps * mean_service_ms / slot_capacity), provision headroom = +40% on steady util to tolerate microbursts.
- Auto-scale guidance:
  - react at 95th-percentile utilization over 30s window (not instantaneous) to avoid thrash from microbursts; ramp rate = +2 slots per 5s (bounded).
  - ephemeral rapid-burst fallback: if queue depth > X (e.g., 8 * slots) for > 2s, open temporary burst slots up to max_slots for 30s.
- Cost-quality tradeoffs:
  - For latency-sensitive customers, prefer lower batch_window_ms + higher slots. This increases GPU cost linearly with slots and non-linearly with smaller batches because batching efficiency drops.
  - For cost-sensitive customers, increase batch_window up to 30 ms and allow higher p95 tail for rare bursts; recommend alerting/SLAs warning instead of strict p95 for 100% of traffic.

Quick antidotes for missed p95s in prod
- If p95 fails during predictable microbursts (e.g., daily peaks), add scheduled headroom windows instead of always-on larger min_slots.
- Implement short-path fallback model (smaller model variant) when queue depth persistence > 5s; route a fraction of requests to fallback to keep p95 SLO intact.

Open questions / TODOs (for next iteration)
- Validate latency_curve numbers against the latest profile from bench-runner (linked PR) for quantized and non-quantized variants.
- Replace sampling sim with a tiny event-driven simulator in the repo for reproducible runs (Marco volunteered to sketch this).
- Decide exact alert thresholds for reactive autoscaler; propose values in next weekly sync (SRE + product).

Action items
- Aisha: push the paramized sheet into /sheets/continuous-batching/queue-shape-probe.csv (export) and share with SRE by 2026-03-05.
- Marco: draft simple event-driven sim and post PR by 2026-03-12 (depends on ENG-4821).
- Lina: run bench-runner on small A100 set and paste latency_curve numbers into tab "latency_curve".

Notes to self (quick):
- This probe intentionally biases conservative towards tail (we care about user-facing p95). Use preferences for lower false negatives when tuning defaults.
- Keep the sheet small: one param tab, one sample-arrival generator, one sim_runs output. That keeps it friendly for product engineers to tweak without heavy infra knowledge.

References (internal)
- see linked confluence page for conceptual doc.
- queueing cheat notes: M/G/k approximations and occupancy correction factors included inline in spreadsheet comments.

If reviewers: please try scenario: steady_rps=18, burst_fraction=0.45, burst_multiplier=8x and send results back.
